Growing food takes months of work, seed, fertiliser and rain. Yet a real share of what is harvested never gets eaten or sold. FAO, the United Nations food and agriculture agency, estimates that about **13 percent of food produced worldwide is lost after harvest and before it reaches retail shelves**. That loss happens on farms, in stores, on lorries and in markets, which means much of it is in the hands of the women who dry, thresh, store, carry and sell food.

This course is about that stretch of the journey: from the moment a crop is harvested until it is eaten or sold. The skills you will learn are called **post-harvest management**. They include drying, cleaning, sorting, storing, cooling, processing and checking food so that more of it stays good for longer.

Every kilogram saved after harvest is a kilogram you already paid for in labour and inputs.
Food loss and food waste are not the same

United Nations agencies use two words. **Food loss** is food that is lost after harvest and before it reaches the shop: grain eaten by weevils in the store, yams that rot in the barn, tomatoes crushed on a lorry. **Food waste** is food thrown away by shops, restaurants and households. The world has a shared goal on both: Sustainable Development Goal target 12.3 asks countries, by 2030, to halve per capita food waste at retail and consumer level and to reduce food losses along production and supply chains, including post-harvest losses. In this course we focus on loss, because that is the part a farmer, trader or processor can control directly.

Loss is not only weight. A bag of beans full of weevil holes may still weigh almost the same, but a buyer offers a lower price, or the family throws part of it away. So when we talk about loss, we think about three things: **weight lost**, **quality lost** (lower grade, lower price) and sometimes **safety lost**, when mould makes food unsafe to eat.
Worked example: tracing losses on one cowpea harvest

For example, Hauwa farms cowpea (beans) near Kano. Last season she harvested about 1,000 kg. She sat down with her daughter and estimated, stage by stage, how much never reached the buyer or the family pot.
Harvest and field drying: some pods were picked late and split open, spilling seed. She estimates 40 kg lost.
Threshing and cleaning: beating the pods on bare ground scattered and broke grain. She estimates 30 kg lost.
Storage for six months in ordinary woven sacks: weevils damaged the beans and she sorted out and threw away about 150 kg.
Transport and market: torn sacks spilled about 10 kg.
Total: 40 + 30 + 150 + 10 = 230 kg. As a share of the harvest: 230 divided by 1,000 = 0.23, which is 23 percent.
Storage alone: 150 divided by 230 = about 0.65, so roughly 65 percent of all her loss happened in the store.
Value: if beans sell for about 1,500 naira per kg (approximate, prices vary by season and market), 230 kg is worth about 345,000 naira.
Hauwa now knows that storage is her biggest loss point. Improving storage first will protect far more beans than working on threshing first.
Estimates are fine at the start
You do not need perfect numbers on day one. A careful estimate written down is much more useful than a vague feeling. In Lesson 3 you will learn simple ways to measure your loss more accurately.
Why the biggest loss point comes first

Many people try to fix everything at once and run out of money and energy. A better approach is to find the stage that loses the most and improve that one first. For a grain or legume farmer, this is very often storage, because grain sits in the store for months while insects multiply. For someone selling fresh vegetables, the biggest loss is often the hours between harvest and sale, when produce wilts in heat. For a fish processor, it can be the time between landing and smoking. The rest of this course follows that order: understand why food spoils, measure your loss, fix the biggest point, then prove that the fix worked.

Harvested food is still alive. A yam in a barn, a bundle of ugu leaves, and even a dry cowpea seed are living things that breathe slowly. Once you understand what makes them break down, choosing the right storage or preservation method becomes much easier. There are five main causes of spoilage, and almost every loss you see comes from one or more of them.
A single water droplet
Moisture is the main driver of mould and insect damage in stored grains and legumes.
Durable and perishable produce

**Durable produce** is low in water when properly dried: grains such as maize, sorghum, millet and rice, legumes such as cowpea and soybean, and groundnuts. Dried well, they can be stored for many months. **Perishable produce** is high in water: leafy vegetables, tomatoes, peppers, garden egg, fruit, fresh fish and roots and tubers such as yam and cassava. These last days or weeks, not months. Durable crops are mostly protected by drying and good storage. Perishables are mostly protected by gentle handling, cooling and fast sale or processing.

These causes feed each other. Damp grain breathes faster, which makes heat, which helps insects and mould grow, which makes more moisture. That is why a small damp patch in a store can turn into a spoiled bag within weeks. For fresh produce, a bruise speeds up breathing in that spot and opens a door for rot, which then spreads to neighbouring produce in the basket.
Mould on grain can be a health risk, not just a nuisance

WHO explains that certain moulds produce aflatoxins, which can damage the liver and are linked to liver cancer. They affect cereals such as maize, sorghum and rice, and oilseeds such as groundnuts, especially in warm, humid conditions. Prevention is efficient drying, keeping crops dry, and proper storage. Grain or nuts that look mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled should be discarded, not eaten, sold or fed to children.
Drying: why weight goes down and that is normal

When you dry grain, it gets lighter because water leaves it. This is not loss: the dry part, called the **dry matter**, stays the same. Many farmers and buyers talk about **moisture content**, the percentage of the grain's weight that is water. Your state's Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension officer, or a grain moisture meter, can tell you the safe storage moisture level for your crop. The calculation below shows how to predict the weight after drying so you are not surprised when you weigh.
Worked example: predicting weight after drying sorghum
For example, Ladi in Kaduna has 500 kg of freshly threshed sorghum. A moisture meter at her cooperative reads 20 percent. The target she has been given for safe storage is 13 percent.
Find the dry matter: 100 minus 20 = 80 percent of the weight is dry matter. 500 kg x 0.80 = 400 kg of dry matter.
At the target, dry matter will be 100 minus 13 = 87 percent of the weight.
Weight after drying = 400 divided by 0.87 = about 459.8 kg, call it 460 kg.
Water removed = 500 minus 459.8 = about 40.2 kg.

Ladi should expect about 460 kg after drying. The 40 kg that disappears is water, not lost food. If she stored the sorghum at 20 percent to avoid that weight drop, she would risk losing far more to mould and insects.

This calculation also helps when you buy or sell. Grain sold wet weighs more but is worth less per kilogram of real food, and it will not keep. Proper drying protects quality and gives you an honest weight.
Roots, tubers and fresh produce

Yams can store for months if they are whole, undamaged and kept cool, shaded and ventilated, for example in a traditional yam barn. Cassava is very different: once dug up, roots start to deteriorate within a few days, which is why many farmers leave cassava in the ground until they are ready to sell or process it. Leafy vegetables such as ugu and waterleaf lose water very fast and wilt within hours in the sun. Each of these behaviours comes straight from the five causes above.
Durable crops need drying and sealed storage; perishables need gentle handling, cooling and speed.
Moisture, breathing, damage, pests and heat cause almost all spoilage, and they feed each other.

Before you change anything, you need a **baseline**: a measured starting point. Without it you cannot prove later that your new method worked. A baseline also stops you from spending money on the wrong problem. This lesson gives you two simple measuring tools, one for stored grains and legumes and one for fresh produce, and a checklist for your store.
A balance scale
A kitchen scale and a notebook are enough to measure your own loss.
Step 1: take a fair sample

You cannot check every bean in a bag, so you take a sample. A fair sample comes from several places, not just the top where grain is often driest and cleanest. Take small handfuls from the top, middle and bottom of a bag, or from several bags, mix them on a clean cloth, then take your working sample from the mix.
Use a clean, dry cup or tin to take about the same amount from the top, middle and bottom of each bag you check.
Pour everything onto a clean cloth or tray and mix well with your hands.
Spread the mix flat, divide it into four parts, and keep one part as your working sample.
Label it with the date, bag number and storage time so far.
Step 2: the count-and-weigh method for grain and legumes

Insects such as weevils and bruchids eat beans and grains from the inside. Counting holed grains tells you how many are damaged, but not how much weight is gone. The **count-and-weigh method**, widely used in post-harvest research, compares the weight of damaged and undamaged grains to estimate the true weight lost. You need a kitchen scale that reads in grams.
Separate the sample into undamaged grains and damaged grains (with holes, tunnels or insect powder).
Count both groups. Call them Nu (number undamaged) and Nd (number damaged).
Weigh both groups in grams. Call them Wu and Wd.
Weight loss percent = (Wu x Nd minus Wd x Nu) divided by (Wu x (Nu + Nd)), then multiply by 100.
Worked example: checking a bag of stored cowpea
For example, Hauwa has about 800 kg of cowpea left in her store after five months. She takes a fair sample and sorts it on a tray with her daughter.
Undamaged: Nu = 420 grains weighing Wu = 84.0 g. Damaged: Nd = 180 grains weighing Wd = 27.0 g.
Damaged by count: 180 divided by 600 total grains = 0.30, so 30 percent of grains are holed.
Bottom of the formula: 84.0 x 600 = 50,400.
Weight loss = 3,780 divided by 50,400 = 0.075, which is 7.5 percent.
Her store now holds 800 kg, so it started at about 800 divided by (1 minus 0.075) = about 865 kg. About 65 kg has been eaten by insects.
Hauwa's beans have lost about 7.5 percent of their weight, but 30 percent of grains are damaged, which will also lower her selling price. Both numbers go in her baseline record.
Two numbers, two stories

Weight loss tells you how much food has gone. Percent damaged grains tells you how much the quality and price will suffer. A buyer looking at a handful of holed beans judges by the damaged count, so record both.

For each harvest or market trip, record what you started with, what sold at full price, what sold at a discount, and what was thrown away or eaten at home because it could not be sold. For grains and legumes, three rules protect almost everything: **store it dry, store it clean, store it sealed**. Each rule blocks one of the main causes of loss you met in Module 1. Dry grain resists mould. Clean grain and a clean store give insects nowhere to hide. Sealed grain stops insects breathing and rats eating.
A pile of beans
Cowpea and other legumes keep for many months when stored dry, clean and sealed.
Rule 1: store it dry, and test it

Never store by guessing. Grain can feel dry on the outside while the inside is still damp. A moisture meter gives a reading in percent and some cooperatives and extension offices have one. If you do not have access to a meter, the **salt jar test** is a simple check that has been promoted by post-harvest programmes in Africa for years.
Dry some table salt in a dry pot over low heat for a few minutes, then let it cool completely.
Fill a clean, completely dry glass jar about one third full with grain from a fair sample.
Add two or three spoons of the dry salt, close the lid tightly and shake for two to three minutes.
Leave it to stand for about fifteen minutes, then look at the sides of the jar.
If salt sticks to the glass, the grain is still too damp to store. Dry it more and test again. If the salt stays loose, the grain is dry enough.
Dry on a clean surface

Dry grain on tarpaulins, mats or a clean concrete floor, never on bare soil. Soil carries mould spores and stones, and grain on the ground picks up damp at night. Cover or bring grain in before rain and before evening dew.
Rule 2: store it clean
Winnow and sort out broken grains, stones, chaff and any mouldy or holed grains before storing. Broken grains are where insects start.
Sweep the store and remove every bit of last season's grain and dust.
Repair roof leaks and block rat holes with cement or tightly packed metal mesh.
Stack bags on pallets or planks raised off the floor, with space between bags and walls so you can inspect all sides.
Rule 3: store it sealed

**Hermetic storage** means airtight storage. When dry grain is sealed in an airtight container, the insects inside and the grain itself keep breathing and use up the oxygen. Carbon dioxide builds up. Without enough oxygen, insects stop feeding and die, so they cannot multiply. No insecticide is needed. Hermetic options include triple-layer hermetic bags, airtight plastic or metal drums, and metal silos.

A well-known example is the **PICS bag (Purdue Improved Crop Storage)** from Purdue University: a triple-layer bag, with two inner plastic liners inside an outer woven bag, designed so low-resource farmers can keep dry crops with minimal insect loss and without insecticides. Other brands of hermetic bag are also sold in Nigeria through agro-dealers.

Storage chemicals and fumigants

If you use any storage insecticide, use only a product registered by NAFDAC for stored grain, follow the label exactly, and never use cotton or field sprays on food. Fumigation tablets (phosphine) release a highly poisonous gas that can kill: they must only be used by trained, licensed fumigators, never in a house or a room where people sleep. Hermetic storage avoids this risk entirely.
Worked example: is it worth buying hermetic bags?

For example, Hauwa plans to store 1,000 kg of cowpea, about ten 100 kg bags. A local agro-dealer sells hermetic bags for about 3,500 naira each (approximate; check current prices). Beans sell for about 1,500 naira per kg (approximate).
Cost of bags: 10 x 3,500 = 35,000 naira.
Break-even: 35,000 divided by 1,500 = about 23.3 kg of beans. The bags pay for themselves if they save just 23.3 kg in one season.
As a share of her store: 23.3 divided by 1,000 = about 2.3 percent.
Her baseline from Module 1 showed about 7.5 percent weight loss after five months, plus 30 percent holed grains that cut her price.
If she reuses undamaged bags for a second season, the cost is shared across two harvests and the break-even halves.
Because her measured loss is far above 2.3 percent, the bags are very likely to pay for themselves in the first season. She will check the result with the count-and-weigh method in Lesson 3.

The same break-even method works for any storage investment: a drum, a silo share, a pallet set or a cooperative store. Divide the cost by the price per kilogram to find how many kilograms it must save, then compare that with your measured loss.

Fresh produce cannot be dried and sealed like grain without changing what it is. To keep it fresh, you slow down its breathing and protect it from bruises. Most of this costs little money. It costs attention: when you harvest, where you put produce, and how you pack it.
A bunch of leafy green vegetables
Leafy vegetables lose water within hours in the sun, so shade and speed matter most.
A cool, gentle harvest-to-sale routine
Harvest day for fresh produce
Harvest in cool early morning
Shade within minutes
Sort out damaged produce
Pack firmly, not tightly
Sell same day or cool
Each step removes heat or damage before it can start rot.
**Harvest early.** Produce picked in the cool morning carries less field heat and wilts more slowly than produce picked at midday.
**Shade immediately.** Put harvested produce under a tree, shed or wet sack straight away, never in direct sun at the edge of the field.
**Sort before packing.** Take out bruised, cut, diseased or over-ripe pieces. Use them at home the same day or process them. One rotten tomato or garden egg can spread rot to its neighbours.
**Handle gently.** Do not throw or drop produce. Do not overfill sacks or stand on loads in vehicles.
**Pack for air.** Use containers with firm sides and gaps for air. Line baskets with clean leaves or paper to cushion produce.
**Keep leafy vegetables damp and shaded.** Sprinkle with clean water and cover with a clean, damp cloth. Do not soak them in dirty water.
The clay pot cooler

Water cools as it evaporates. You feel this when wet skin dries in a breeze. A **clay pot cooler**, also called a pot-in-pot cooler, uses this to keep vegetables cooler than the air around them without electricity. It works best in dry, breezy weather, as in much of northern Nigeria during the dry season, and works less well when the air is very humid.
Get two unglazed clay pots, one small enough to sit inside the other with a gap of a few centimetres all round.
Put a layer of clean sand in the bottom of the big pot, stand the small pot on it, and fill the gap around the sides with sand.
Pour clean water into the sand until it is wet but not flooded.
Put produce in the inner pot and cover it with a damp cloth.
Keep the cooler in shade where air moves, and add water to the sand once or twice a day.
Put a simple thermometer inside and another outside for a few days, and write down the difference so you know what your cooler actually achieves.
Measure, do not assume

How much cooler the pot keeps depends on your weather. Record the inside and outside temperature for a week before you rely on it for sales, and compare how long your produce lasts with and without it.
Yam and cassava

**Yam** stores for months if handled with care. Harvest without cutting or bruising tubers, let small wounds dry in shade before storage, and keep yams in a cool, shaded, well-ventilated place such as a raised yam barn or open shed, not piled on damp ground. Check regularly, remove any rotting tubers at once, and rub off sprouts. A cut yam will not store, so use or process it quickly.

**Cassava** roots begin to deteriorate within a few days of being dug up. The practical approach is to leave cassava in the ground until you are ready to sell or process it, and to harvest only what can be peeled and processed into garri, fufu, chips or flour within about a day or two.
Worked example: does a clay pot cooler pay for itself?

For example, Grace sells ugu (fluted pumpkin leaves) in Makurdi. Her baseline: she takes 30 bundles to market, sells 22 at about 300 naira each (approximate), and the 8 left over wilt overnight and are thrown away.

Storing food is not a one-time job. Problems start small: a few insects on the surface, a warm patch in a bag, a musty smell. If you catch them early, you can save most of the store. If you open the store only when you need to sell, you may find the damage already done. This lesson gives you a routine and shows you how to prove, with your own numbers, that a new method really works.

A fair before-and-after comparison
To prove a change works, compare like with like. Otherwise a good result might just be a dry year or a shorter storage time.
Same crop and, if possible, the same variety.
Same storage length: compare five months with five months.
Same measuring method: count-and-weigh both times, or the same trip record.
If you can, run both methods side by side in the same season, for example two ordinary bags next to two hermetic bags filled with the same grain on the same day.
Worked example: valuing a loss reduction

For example, Hauwa stored 1,000 kg of cowpea in ordinary sacks last year and measured 7.5 percent weight loss after five months. This year she stored 1,000 kg in hermetic bags costing 35,000 naira in total and checked after five months with the same method.
Last year's weight loss: 1,000 x 0.075 = 75 kg.
This year's count-and-weigh result: 1.0 percent, so 1,000 x 0.01 = 10 kg.
Beans saved: 75 minus 10 = 65 kg.
Value saved at about 1,500 naira per kg (approximate): 65 x 1,500 = 97,500 naira.
Minus the cost of the bags: 97,500 minus 35,000 = 62,500 naira net gain in the first season, before counting the better price for cleaner beans.
Hauwa has written proof, measured the same way both years, that hermetic storage gave her a net gain of about 62,500 naira, plus bags she can check and reuse.
When a good method seems to fail

Sometimes a farmer tries hermetic bags or a new routine and reports that it did not work. Before you give up on a method, check whether one of these common mistakes caused the poor result. Most failures come from how the method was used, not from the method itself.
Grain was sealed before it was dry enough, so mould grew inside the bag.
A liner had a small hole, or the ties were loose, so oxygen kept coming in.
Bags were opened every week to take beans for cooking, letting fresh air in each time. Keep a separate small container for daily use.
Rats chewed the bags because they were stored on the floor in an untidy store.
Grain was already heavily infested and was not cleaned before sealing, so damage started early.
The before and after checks were done at different storage times, so the numbers could not be compared.

Notice that she also gained on quality: fewer holed beans means a better grade. If buyers paid her more per kilogram, add that difference too, but only if you recorded the actual prices. Keep every record in one notebook or a phone note per season, with dates. Over two or three seasons this becomes your own evidence, more reliable than general advice.

Solar drying: cleaner than open sun

Open sun drying on the ground exposes food to dust, insects, birds, goats and sudden rain. A **solar dryer** is a box or tent with a clear plastic or glass cover and air vents. The sun heats the air inside, and moving air carries moisture away. The cover keeps out dust, insects, animals and rain. You can build a simple one from a wooden frame, clear UV-resistant plastic sheeting and food-safe mesh trays. Raise trays off the ground, leave air gaps, and turn the produce so it dries evenly.
Wash hands and all tools. Peel and slice on a clean board, not on the floor.
Cut pieces to an even thickness so they dry at the same rate.
Spread in one thin layer on clean mesh trays, raised off the ground.
Dry until pieces are hard and snap cleanly. Any soft or bendy piece needs more time.
Cool, then pack at once in clean, dry, airtight containers or sealed bags, labelled with product and date.
Check stored chips regularly; discard any batch that shows mould.
Smoke and fish

When fat from fish drips onto open flames, or fish sits in thick, dirty smoke, harmful compounds called PAHs build up on the fish. Improved smoking kilns keep the fire separate from the fish and catch dripping fat. Whatever kiln you use, keep flames away from the fish, use clean dry wood, and never burn plastic, rubber or painted wood.
Worked example: damaged yams, sell at a discount or dry into chips?

For example, Funmi farms yam near Oyo. At harvest, 60 of her tubers were cut by the hoe. Cut yams will not store, so she must decide this week. Buyers offer about 1,000 naira each for damaged tubers (approximate). Her 60 tubers weigh about 150 kg, an average of 2.5 kg each.
Option A, sell now: 60 x 1,000 = 60,000 naira.
Option B, a small trial first: she peels, slices, parboils and dries 10 kg of yam and gets 2.5 kg of dry chips, a yield of 25 percent in her hands.
Expected chips from 150 kg: 150 x 0.25 = 37.5 kg.
Local buyers of chips for elubo offer about 2,500 naira per kg (approximate): 37.5 x 2,500 = 93,750 naira.
Her costs for firewood, labour help, transport and bags come to about 15,000 naira: 93,750 minus 15,000 = 78,750 naira.
Difference: 78,750 minus 60,000 = 18,750 naira more for processing, and dry chips can be sold over several weeks instead of in one rush.

Processing pays for Funmi, but only because she measured her own yield and costs first. If chip prices had been lower or she had no time for drying, selling at a discount the same day would still have been better than letting the yams rot.

You do not have time or labour for the drying days, and nobody can help.
Your trial yield or quality is poor, for example chips that stay soft or turn mouldy.
There is no buyer for the processed product at a price above your fresh discount price plus costs.
You cannot keep the product clean and dry while it waits for sale.

Six parts, each one short and backed by records.

Percent and percentage points

If your loss falls from 12 percent to 5 percent, it has fallen by **7 percentage points**. That is different from saying it fell by 7 percent. Using percentage points avoids confusion when you report your results.
Worked example: a garden egg project summary

For example, Ifeoma grows garden egg near Nsukka and takes about 50 kg to market on each trip. Her baseline over three trips: about 6 kg per trip thrown away or sold for almost nothing because of bruising and soft spots.
Baseline loss: 6 divided by 50 = 0.12, which is 12 percent.
Change: harvest before 8 am, keep the harvest in shade, sort out damaged fruit for home use, line baskets with leaves and stop stacking sacks on top of baskets in the bus.
Result over three trips, same record method: about 2.5 kg lost per trip. 2.5 divided by 50 = 0.05, which is 5 percent.
Reduction: 12 minus 5 = 7 percentage points, or 6 minus 2.5 = 3.5 kg saved per trip.
Value at about 1,200 naira per kg (approximate): 3.5 x 1,200 = 4,200 naira per trip. Over 12 trips in the next 90 days that is about 4,200 x 12 = 50,400 naira, at almost no extra cost.

Common mistakes in project reports
Measuring the result after a shorter storage time than the baseline, which makes the improvement look bigger than it is.
Forgetting to subtract the cost of bags, coolers or labour from the value saved.
Using an exact-looking price without saying it is approximate or where it came from.
Reporting a single good market day instead of the average of several trips.
Leaving out photos or dates, so nobody can check the record.
Check your own pack against this list before you present it. A careful, modest result that anyone can check is more valuable than a large result that cannot be trusted.
Honesty makes your evidence stronger
If a change did not work, say so and explain what you learned. A partner or lender trusts a record that shows real numbers, including disappointments, far more than one that only shows success.

Ifeoma's plan, for example, is specific. In weeks 1 to 4 she uses her new handling routine on every trip and keeps her trip records. In weeks 5 to 8 she builds a clay pot cooler for leftover fruit and measures how many extra she sells the next day. In weeks 9 to 12 she shows four other garden egg sellers at her market how she sorts and packs, and helps each of them keep three trip records. In week 13 she updates her pack with all the new numbers. Each action has a time, a person and a measure, so she can tell at the end whether she did it.

Why this matters
Food you grew, but never ate or sold
About 13 percent of food is lost after harvest
Food loss: before the shop. Food waste: after
Loss is weight, quality, and sometimes safety
Measure first, then fix the biggest loss point

Growing food takes months of work, seed and rain. Yet FAO, the United Nations food agency, estimates that about 13 percent of food produced worldwide is lost after harvest, before it reaches the shops.
Food lost on farms, in stores, on lorries and in markets is called food loss. Food thrown away by shops and homes is food waste. We focus on loss, because that is the part you can control.
Loss is not only weight. Beans full of weevil holes may weigh almost the same, but the buyer pays less. And mould can make food unsafe.
In this module you learn to find your loss, measure it, and choose where to act first.
Every crop passes through these stages
Every crop moves through a chain. At harvest and field drying, late picking splits pods, and rain, birds and goats take their share.
Beating pods on bare ground scatters and breaks grain. In storage, weevils, mould and rats do the damage.
On the road, overloaded sacks crush produce, and in the market it wilts before it sells. So you check each stage instead of guessing.
Worked example
Hauwa traces her cowpea losses
Fix the biggest loss point first.
Harvest and field drying: 40 kg lost
Threshing and cleaning: 30 kg lost
Storage in woven sacks: 150 kg lost
Transport and market: 10 kg lost
Total 230 kg out of 1,000 kg: 23 percent
For example, Hauwa farms cowpea near Kano. Last season she harvested about 1,000 kg. She sat with her daughter and estimated the loss at each stage.
Pods picked late split open, about 40 kg. Threshing on bare ground, about 30 kg.
Six months in ordinary woven sacks, and weevils spoiled about 150 kg. Torn sacks on the way to market spilled about 10 kg.
Add them up: 230 kg. Divide by 1,000, and that is 23 percent of her harvest. At about 1,500 naira per kg, that is roughly 345,000 naira.
Storage alone was about 65 percent of her loss. So she fixes storage first. Do not try to fix everything at once and run out of money and energy.
Know your product
Durable or perishable?
Durable
Dried grains and legumes
Risks: damp, insects, rats
Protect: dry and seal
Perishable
Fresh produce, fish, yam
Risks: bruising, heat, rot
Protect: shade, cool, sell fast
Harvested food is still alive and breathing. Durable produce, like maize, cowpea and groundnuts, is low in water once dried. Protect it by drying and sealed storage.
Perishable produce, like tomatoes, ugu, fish and yam, is high in water. It is protected by gentle handling, cooling and fast sale.
Why food spoils
Five causes that feed each other
Mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled grain: throw it away.
Moisture: damp grain grows mould
Breathing: produce shrivels and loses taste
Damage: cuts and bruises let rot in
Pests: weevils, bruchids and rats
Heat: makes everything faster
Almost every loss comes from five causes. Moisture lets mould grow. Breathing uses up the produce's own sugars and water.
Bruises let rot in. Pests eat from the inside. And heat speeds up all of it. They feed each other, so a small damp patch can spoil a bag within weeks.

Here is the safety rule. Some moulds make aflatoxins, which WHO links to liver damage and liver cancer. Grain or nuts that look mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled must be discarded, not eaten, sold or fed to children.

When Hauwa checked her store after five months, 30 percent of her beans were holed, and the weight loss was 7.5 percent. Record both. Holes cut the price, weight loss cuts the stock.

Three rules
What protects grains and legumes
Store it dry: damp grain grows mould
Store it clean: insects start in dirt and broken grain
Store it sealed: no air for insects, no way in for rats
Then measure again to prove it worked
For grains and legumes, three rules protect almost everything. Store it dry, store it clean, store it sealed. Each rule blocks one of the causes of loss from Module 1.
Then you check your store regularly, and measure again the same way, so your own numbers show whether the change paid.
Rule 1: test, never guess
The salt jar test
Salt sticks to the glass? Too damp. Dry it more.
Dry table salt in a pot, then cool it
Fill a dry glass jar one third with grain
Add two or three spoons of salt, shake
Wait about fifteen minutes
Look at the sides of the jar
Grain can feel dry outside while the inside is still damp. If you have no moisture meter, use the salt jar test.
Dry some table salt over low heat and let it cool. Fill a clean, completely dry glass jar about one third full of grain from a fair sample.
Add two or three spoons of the dry salt, close the lid tightly, and shake for two to three minutes. Leave it for about fifteen minutes.
If salt sticks to the glass, the grain is still too damp. Dry it more and test again. If the salt stays loose, it is dry enough.
Always dry on tarpaulins or mats, never on bare soil.
Rule 3: sealed
Filling a hermetic bag
Do not open the bags often. Keep a small tin for daily use.
Check each liner against the light for holes
Inner liner inside middle, inside woven bag
Fill with dry, clean grain only
Squeeze out air, twist, fold and tie each layer
Store on pallets, away from rats and sun
Hermetic means airtight. Sealed in, the insects use up the oxygen, stop feeding and die. No insecticide is needed. But first clean the grain and sweep out last season's dust.
Check each liner against the light, and never use a torn one. Put the liners inside the woven bag and fill with dry, clean grain.
Squeeze out the air, twist each liner tightly, fold it over and tie it firmly. Store the bags on pallets, away from sharp edges and rats.
When people say the bags failed, it is usually how they were used. Grain sealed while damp, a small hole, loose ties, or opening the bag every week for cooking.
Safety first
Chemicals and hygiene
Phosphine gas can kill. Only trained, licensed fumigators. Never in a house or a sleeping room.
Only NAFDAC-registered products for stored grain, used as the label says. Never field sprays.
Use clean water on vegetables and coolers. Wash hands and clean containers between uses.
Three safety points. Fumigation tablets release a highly poisonous gas. Only trained, licensed fumigators may use them, and never where people live or sleep.
If you use a storage insecticide, use only one registered by NAFDAC for stored grain, and follow the label exactly. Never use cotton or field sprays on food. Hermetic storage avoids this risk.
And dirty water spreads germs, even when produce looks fresh. Use clean water, wash your hands, and clean baskets between uses.
Fresh produce
Cool and gentle, from field to market
Do
Harvest in the cool early morning
Sort out bruised pieces first
Firm containers with air gaps
Don't
Leave produce in the sun
Throw, drop or stand on loads
Overfill sacks
Soak leaves in dirty water

Fresh produce cannot be sealed like grain. You slow its breathing and protect it from bruises. Harvest early, shade it fast, and sort out damaged pieces, because one rotten tomato spreads rot to its neighbours.
Do not throw it, overfill sacks, or stand on loads. Keep yams whole and ventilated, and dig cassava only when you can process it within a day or two.
Monitoring
Check your store on a routine
Every two weeks: look and smell
Every month: sample and count-and-weigh
Hermetic bags: check for holes, do not open
Fresh produce and yams: every few days
Problems start small. Every two weeks, walk the store. Look for insects, powder, droppings, chewed bags and damp. Smell for mustiness.
Every month, sample open bags with the count-and-weigh check. Grain that feels warm deep inside is a warning sign.
Do not open hermetic bags for checks. Look for holes and loose ties instead. Check fresh produce and yams every few days, and remove anything soft or mouldy at once.

Value addition
Five ways to make food last longer
Drying: yam chips, cassava chips, okra
Smoking: catfish, mackerel
Salting: salted dried fish
Fermenting: garri, fufu, iru
Cooling: leafy vegetables, fish on ice
Some produce will not store fresh. Yams cut by the hoe, cassava that must be used within days, fish landed in the heat. Instead of watching it rot, you can turn it into a product that lasts.
Drying removes the water that moulds need. Smoking dries and coats the food. Salting draws water out and stops many germs.
Fermenting uses friendly microbes, as in garri and iru. And cooling slows breathing and germ growth.
Clean solar drying
Drying chips safely
Soft or bendy pieces need more time. Mould means discard.
Wash hands and tools, slice on a clean board
Cut pieces to an even thickness
One thin layer on raised mesh trays
Dry until pieces are hard and snap
Cool, pack airtight, label with date
Check stored chips regularly
Open sun drying on the ground lets in dust, insects, goats and rain. A solar dryer is a box or tent with a clear cover and air vents. The cover keeps all of that out.
Wash your hands and tools, and slice on a clean board, not the floor. Cut pieces evenly so they dry at the same rate, and spread them thinly on raised trays.
Dry until each piece snaps cleanly. Cool, then pack at once in clean, airtight containers, labelled with the product and date.
Any soft piece needs more time. And any batch that shows mould must be thrown away.
Smoking fish safely
Keep the fire away from the fish
Do
Keep flames away from the fish
Catch the dripping fat
Burn clean, dry wood
Never
Let fat drip onto open flames
Smoke in thick, dirty smoke
Burn plastic, tyres or painted wood
When fat drips onto flames, or fish sits in thick dirty smoke, harmful compounds called PAHs build up on the fish. Improved kilns keep the fire separate and catch the fat.
Whatever kiln you use, never burn plastic, rubber, tyres or painted wood.

Cost of the change subtracted
Prices marked approximate
Average of several trips
